The Problem

Pain that functions.
People who don't.

"I sat through a 3-hour exam with cramps so bad I couldn't see straight. I just smiled and said I was fine."

— Contextual Interview, Participant 04 · College student, 21

79%
reported no institutional support during severe menstrual pain episodes in public spaces.
87%
never disclosed pain to their institution — not from preference, but because there was no safe, dignified pathway to do so.
Research Snapshot

What the data
couldn't stay silent about

79% no institutional support during episodes
68% felt unsafe or unwelcoming in public spaces
91% unaware of any campus wellness resources
3.2× more likely to leave than to seek help

P07 · Working professional

P11 · Undergraduate

Core Insights

From pain to
design principles

01
Invisibility is survival — not preferenceIdentity & Behavior
"Drawing attention to pain felt more dangerous than the pain itself."
Design response: Build support that requires zero explanation — silent, contextual, always available.
02
The body already knows — tech just needs to listenPatterns & Prediction
"People track cycles informally but lack tools to recognize their own patterns."
Design response: Predictive 7-day prep cycles from logged data — agency before pain strikes.
03
Support infrastructure exists but stays disconnectedSystems & Access
"Institutions have nurses, quiet rooms, HR — but no pathway connects them to the person in pain."
Design response: An ecosystem layer bridging person, caregiver, institution, and real space — in real time.

Accessibility

Designing beyond
the average user

🤫
Non-Verbal Interaction
All critical pain-mode actions are gesture-driven or single-tap. No typing required when pain is severe.
🔕
Silent SOS
Request support without speaking or explaining. The system handles communication automatically.
👁️
Sensory-Sensitive Design
Dim mode, reduced animation, larger targets — all auto-activated in Pain Mode to reduce sensory load.
🔒
Privacy Masking
Screen displays a neutral "Wellness Check" facade. No one nearby needs to know what app you're using.
⚡
Low-Effort Interactions
Designed for a user in pain. Every key action requires 1–2 taps. No deep navigation when you're suffering.
♿
Inclusive Space Filters
Pause Spaces filtered by wheelchair access, tactile wayfinding, and assistive features — for all bodies.
Pause Space

A physical refuge
designed for dignity

Indirect Warm Lighting
Soft, dimmable lighting designed to create a calm, safe environment. Adjustable via the in-space control panel.
Acoustic Panelling
Sound-absorbing walls for privacy and noise reduction — a genuinely quiet space in a noisy institution.
Targeted Pain Relief Zones
Heat therapy (abdomen), pressure/vibration (back), and vibration (thighs/legs) for targeted physical relief.
Easy-Reach Control Panel
Heat level, pulse intensity, light, breathing guide, and session timer — all accessible without standing up.

Impact & Reflection

What Pause
could change

🌱
Expected Impact
Reduce institutional absences due to menstrual pain by creating an accessible, real-time support layer. Give people the tools to be seen — or stay invisible — entirely on their own terms.
💡
Key Learnings
The most powerful design choices were subtractive — removing friction, removing shame, removing the need to explain. The deepest UX insight: designing for extreme users creates better experiences for everyone.
🔭
Future Scope
Wearable integration for passive pain detection. Institutional dashboards for anonymous aggregate health data. Expansion to all invisible chronic pain conditions.

"Design doesn't just solve problems.
At its best, it dissolves the shame that made the problem invisible."

Pause started as a question: why do people suffer alone in institutions built to support them? The answer wasn't technology — it was trust. And trust is designed, not assumed. This project taught me that the most important thing a designer can do is listen to what people don't say.
